title: Definite articles el / la / los / las
micro_note: Spanish nouns are masculine or feminine. Definite articles match both gender and number: el/los for masculine, la/las for feminine. Use them for specific things and general categories.
contrast_a_en: The book is here.
contrast_b_en: The houses are big.

title: Indefinite articles un / una / unos / unas
micro_note: Use un/una for 'a/an' and unos/unas for 'some' or approximate numbers. Unlike English, omit un/una before unmodified professions after ser.
contrast_a_en: I need a coffee.
contrast_b_en: I bought some apples.

title: Mandatory contractions al and del
micro_note: Whenever the prepositions a or de sit directly before the masculine singular article el, they fuse obligatorily into al and del. Never fuse them with él (he) or la.
contrast_a_en: I am going to the park now.
contrast_b_en: I am coming from work.

title: Noun pluralization -s and -es
micro_note: Nouns ending in an unstressed vowel add -s; nouns ending in a consonant or stressed -í/-ú add -es. Final -z changes to -ces before adding the plural ending.
contrast_a_en: The light is on.
contrast_b_en: The lights are on.

title: Masculine el before stressed feminine a-
micro_note: Feminine singular nouns starting with a stressed a- or ha- (like agua, hambre, águila) take el/un to avoid colliding vowels, yet remain feminine for adjectives and plurals.
contrast_a_en: The cold water is tasty.
contrast_b_en: The cold waters flow fast.

title: Subject pronouns and pro-drop omission
micro_note: Spanish verb endings already identify the subject, so subject pronouns (yo, tú, él) are normally dropped. Include them for contrast, emphasis, or disambiguation.
contrast_a_en: I speak Spanish every day.
contrast_b_en: I speak, while you listen.

title: Informal tú vs formal usted
micro_note: Use tú with friends, peers, and family. Use usted with third-person singular verb forms to show respect or formal distance with strangers, elders, or officials.
contrast_a_en: How are you today? (informal)
contrast_b_en: How are you today? (formal)

title: Ser for identity, profession, and origin
micro_note: Use ser to define what or who someone is: name, nationality, profession, material, and permanent identity. Omit the indefinite article before an unmodified profession.
contrast_a_en: She is a doctor in Madrid.
contrast_b_en: We are from Mexico.

title: Ser for time, dates, and schedules
micro_note: Telling clock time and dates always uses ser: es for one o'clock and son for all other hours, paired with the feminine article la/las referring to hora(s).
contrast_a_en: It is one thirty.
contrast_b: Son las ocho de la noche.
contrast_b_en: It is eight at night.

title: Estar for physical location of people and objects
micro_note: Physical location of people, buildings, and objects always takes estar—even when permanent like a city or mountain. Reserve ser for where an event takes place.
contrast_a: El museo está en el centro.
contrast_a_en: The museum is downtown.
contrast_b: La fiesta es en mi casa.
contrast_b_en: The party is at my house.

title: Estar for temporary moods and states
micro_note: Use estar for changing conditions, emotions, health states, and results of actions—how someone or something feels or stands at a given moment.
contrast_a_en: I am very tired today.
contrast_b_en: The door is open.

title: Hay for existence vs estar for specific location
micro_note: Hay (there is / there are) introduces unspecified or new things with un, numbers, or bare plurals. Estar locates specific, already-known items with el/la or possessives.
contrast_a: Hay un banco cerca de aquí.
contrast_a_en: There is a bank near here.
contrast_b: El banco está en esa esquina.
contrast_b_en: The bank is on that corner.

title: Regular -ar present indicative verbs
micro_note: Drop -ar and add -o, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an. Spanish present tense covers both habitual actions ('I work') and current actions ('I am working').
contrast_a_en: I work in an office.
contrast_b_en: They speak very fast.

title: Regular -er present indicative verbs
micro_note: Drop -er and add -o, -es, -e, -emos, -éis, -en. Notice the vowel shifts from -a- to -e- across every non-yo ending compared to -ar verbs.
contrast_a_en: I eat fruit in the morning.
contrast_b_en: We drink cold water.

title: Regular -ir present indicative verbs
micro_note: Regular -ir verbs match -er endings except in nosotros (-imos) and vosotros (-ís). Common examples include vivir, escribir, abrir, and recibir.
contrast_a_en: I live near the sea.
contrast_b_en: We live in the same neighborhood.

title: Tener for possession, age, and sensations
micro_note: Tener (tengo, tienes, tiene...) expresses possession, age ('tener X años'), and bodily states like hunger, thirst, cold, heat, and fear where English uses 'to be'.
contrast_a_en: I am thirty years old.
contrast_b_en: You are very cold here.

title: Ir + a + place for movement
micro_note: Ir (voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van) pairs with preposition a to state destinations. Remember a + el contracts to al.
contrast_a_en: I am going to the station now.
contrast_b_en: We are going to the market together.

title: Ir a + infinitive for near future
micro_note: Conjugate ir + a + infinitive to express planned or imminent future actions ('going to do'). This is the most common everyday way to talk about the future in Spanish.
contrast_a_en: I am going to study this afternoon.
contrast_b: Van a cenar a las nueve.
contrast_b_en: They are going to have dinner at nine.

title: Tener que + infinitive for personal obligation
micro_note: Tener que + infinitive expresses personal necessity or obligation ('have to'). Conjugate tener for the subject while leaving the second verb in its infinitive.
contrast_a_en: I have to leave early.
contrast_b_en: You have to read this message.

title: Hay que + infinitive for impersonal obligation
micro_note: Hay que + infinitive states a general rule or impersonal necessity ('one must / you have to') without naming a specific subject.
contrast_a: Hay que pagar antes de entrar.
contrast_a_en: One must pay before entering.
contrast_b_en: I have to pay my bill.

title: Adjective gender and number agreement
micro_note: Adjectives agree with the noun they modify in gender and number, and normally follow the noun. Adjectives ending in -e or a consonant do not change for gender.
contrast_a_en: It is a modern city.
contrast_b_en: They are modern buildings.

title: Shortened pre-noun forms buen, mal, gran, primer
micro_note: Bueno, malo, primero, and tercero drop -o before a masculine singular noun (buen día). Grande shortens to gran before any singular noun, shifting meaning to 'great'.
contrast_a_en: He is a good friend of mine.
contrast_b_en: She had a great idea yesterday.

title: Unstressed possessive determiners mi, tu, su, nuestro
micro_note: Possessive determiners agree with the possessed thing, NOT the owner. Only nuestro/vuestro change for gender; su can mean his, her, your (usted), or their.
contrast_a: Mis llaves están en la mesa.
contrast_a_en: My keys are on the table.
contrast_b_en: Our house has a garden.

title: Three-way demonstratives este, ese, aquel
micro_note: Spanish divides distance into three zones: este (near speaker), ese (near listener), and aquel (far from both). All agree in gender and number with the noun.
contrast_a_en: This coffee is hot.
contrast_b_en: That mountain over there is far.

title: Simple negation with no before the verb
micro_note: Place no directly before the conjugated verb (and before any object pronouns attached to it). Never split no from the verb with adverbs.
contrast_a_en: I do not understand this word.
contrast_b_en: I do not want it now.

title: Yes/no questions via intonation and subject inversion
micro_note: Spanish forms yes/no questions without auxiliary 'do'. Simply use rising intonation (marked by ¿...?) and optionally place the subject after the verb.
contrast_a_en: Do you speak English well?
contrast_b_en: Is María coming tonight?

title: Interrogative words with written accents
micro_note: Question words always carry an accent mark: qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cómo, cuánto, por qué, cuál. Keep any preposition at the very start of the question.
contrast_a_en: Where do you live now?
contrast_b_en: Who do you work with?

title: Qué vs cuál before ser and nouns
micro_note: Use qué to ask for a definition or before a noun ('what book'). Use cuál/cuáles before ser to ask for a specific selection ('what is your name/number').
contrast_a_en: What is this?
contrast_b_en: What is your number?

title: Gustar with indirect object pronouns me/te/le
micro_note: With gustar, the thing liked is the grammatical subject: use gusta for singular nouns or infinitives, gustan for plural nouns, and me/te/le/nos/os/les for the experiencer.
contrast_a_en: I like reading novels.
contrast_b_en: I like classic movies.

title: A mí también / tampoco agreement patterns
micro_note: To agree with a gustar statement, use a mí también (positive) or a mí tampoco (negative). To disagree, flip polarity with a mí sí or a mí no.
contrast_a: Me gusta el té. — A mí también.
contrast_a_en: I like tea. — Me too.
contrast_b: No me gusta el frío. — A mí tampoco.
contrast_b_en: I don't like the cold. — Me neither.

title: Stem-changing verbs e -> ie (querer, pensar, empezar)
micro_note: In e->ie 'boot' verbs, the stressed stem vowel splits to ie in all forms except nosotros and vosotros. Querer, pensar, cerrar, and preferir follow this pattern.
contrast_a_en: I want a one-way ticket.
contrast_b_en: We want to leave soon.

title: Stem-changing verbs o -> ue (poder, volver, dormir)
micro_note: In o->ue verbs, stressed o becomes ue everywhere outside nosotros/vosotros. Jugar follows the same boot pattern with u->ue.
contrast_a_en: I cannot open the door.
contrast_b_en: We can try it tomorrow.

title: Stem-changing verbs e -> i (pedir, servir, seguir)
micro_note: Only -ir verbs take the e->i stem change inside the boot (pido, pides, pide, pedimos, pedís, piden). Common verbs: pedir, repetir, decir, seguir.
contrast_a_en: I always order soup here.
contrast_b_en: We are asking for the check now.

title: Irregular -go yo-forms (hacer, poner, salir, traer)
micro_note: Several high-frequency verbs add -go (or -igo) solely in the yo present form while staying regular in other persons: hago, pongo, salgo, traigo, digo, vengo.
contrast_a: Salgo de casa a las siete.
contrast_a_en: I leave home at seven.
contrast_b_en: She leaves a bit later.

title: Saber vs conocer for 'to know'
micro_note: Use saber (sé) for facts, information, and skills (+ infinitive). Use conocer (conozco) for acquaintance with people, places, and works of art.
contrast_a_en: I know how to swim quite well.
contrast_b_en: I know this city well.

title: Daily-routine reflexive verbs (levantarse, ducharse)
micro_note: Reflexive verbs pair a verb with me/te/se/nos/os/se when the subject acts on itself. With body parts or clothing, Spanish uses definite articles instead of possessives.
contrast_a_en: I get up at six.
contrast_b: Se lava las manos antes de comer.
contrast_b_en: He washes his hands before eating.

title: Core spatial prepositions en, a, de, con, sin
micro_note: En covers both 'in' and 'on'; a marks motion toward; de shows origin or possession; con/sin mean 'with/without'.
contrast_a: El vaso está en la mesa.
contrast_a_en: The glass is on the table.
contrast_b_en: I drink coffee without sugar.

title: Compound location prepositions (delante de, detrás de, al lado de)
micro_note: Locative adverbs pair with de before a noun: delante de, detrás de, encima de, debajo de, cerca de, lejos de, al lado de. Drop de if no noun follows.
contrast_a: La farmacia está al lado del banco.
contrast_a_en: The pharmacy is next to the bank.
contrast_b_en: The cinema is very close.

title: Muy vs mucho / mucha / muchos / muchas
micro_note: Muy is invariable and modifies adjectives or adverbs ('very'). Mucho modifies verbs (invariable) or agrees in gender/number before nouns ('a lot of / many').
contrast_a_en: The trip is very long.
contrast_b_en: I have a lot of work today.

title: Indefinite quantifiers poco, bastante, demasiado, todo
micro_note: Quantifiers before nouns agree in gender and number (pocas personas, demasiada sal), while modifying a verb or adjective they stay masculine singular.
contrast_a_en: There are too many people here.
contrast_b_en: We walked quite a bit yesterday.

title: Estar + gerundio for ongoing actions
micro_note: Combine estar with -ando (-ar verbs) or -iendo (-er/-ir verbs) to describe actions in progress right now. Unlike English, never use estar + gerundio for future plans.
contrast_a_en: I am reading an article.
contrast_b_en: They are eating in the courtyard.

title: Irregular gerunds (-yendo, durmiendo, pidiendo)
micro_note: Stem-changing -ir verbs shift e->i or o->u in the gerund (pidiendo, durmiendo, diciendo). Vowel stems use -yendo (leyendo, oyendo, trayendo).
contrast_a_en: The child is sleeping already.
contrast_b_en: I am reading your email.

title: Poder, querer, deber + infinitive
micro_note: Modal verbs take a bare infinitive directly with NO preposition 'a' or 'de' in between. Object pronouns may precede the modal or attach to the infinitive.
contrast_a_en: I must finish this today.
contrast_b_en: Can you help me a moment?

title: Weather expressions with hacer, haber, and estar
micro_note: Most weather uses impersonal hace + noun (hace frío/calor/sol/viento). Visible phenomena use hay (hay niebla/nubes) or estar + adjective (está nublado).
contrast_a_en: Today it is very windy.
contrast_b_en: It is cloudy and foggy.

title: Personal a before specific human direct objects
micro_note: Place the preposition a before a direct object when it refers to a specific person (or beloved pet). Omit it for things or nonspecific people with tener.
contrast_a: Veo a mi hermana cada domingo.
contrast_a_en: I see my sister every Sunday.
contrast_b_en: I see the mountain from here.

title: Prepositional pronouns mí, ti, conmigo, contigo
micro_note: After prepositions use mí and ti instead of yo and tú (para mí, sin ti). After con, they fuse into conmigo and contigo.
contrast_a_en: This gift is for you.
contrast_b_en: Do you want to come with me?

title: Basic coordinating conjunctions y/e, o/u, pero
micro_note: Use e instead of y before words starting with i-/hi- (padre e hijo), and u instead of o before o-/ho- (siete u ocho) to prevent identical vowels colliding.
contrast_a_en: I study Spanish and Italian.
contrast_b: Llegará en siete u ocho días.
contrast_b_en: It will arrive in seven or eight days.

title: Cause with porque vs question ¿por qué?
micro_note: Two words with accent (¿por qué?) ask 'why?'. One word without accent (porque) answers 'because'. El porqué (with article) is the noun 'the reason'.
contrast_a_en: Why are you arriving so late?
contrast_b: Llego tarde porque perdí el bus.
contrast_b_en: I am late because I missed the bus.

title: Days of the week with el / los
micro_note: Spanish uses el + day for 'on [day]' (no 'en') and los + day for habitual weekly routines ('on Mondays'). Days are masculine and not capitalized.
contrast_a_en: On Tuesday I have an appointment.
contrast_b_en: On Saturdays I cook at home.

title: Frequency adverbs siempre, a veces, casi nunca, nunca
micro_note: When nunca or jamás comes after the verb, Spanish requires no before the verb. When placed before the verb, drop no.
contrast_a: Nunca bebo café por la noche.
contrast_a_en: I never drink coffee at night.
contrast_b: No bebo café nunca por la noche.
contrast_b_en: I never drink coffee at night.

title: Cardinal numbers 0–1000 and gender of uno/cientos
micro_note: Uno shortens to un before masculine nouns and becomes una before feminine ones. Hundreds 200–900 also agree in gender (doscientas páginas).
contrast_a_en: There are twenty-one students.
contrast_b_en: The book has three hundred pages.

title: Ordinal numbers primero through décimo
micro_note: Ordinals agree in gender and number with the noun (la segunda calle, los primeros días). Beyond 10th, everyday Spanish normally uses cardinal numbers.
contrast_a_en: I live on the third floor.
contrast_b: Es la primera vez que vengo.
contrast_b_en: It is the first time I come.

title: Direct object pronouns lo, la, los, las
micro_note: Replace a known direct object noun with lo/la/los/las matching its gender and number, placed directly before a conjugated verb (or attached to an infinitive/gerund).
contrast_a_en: Are you buying the bread? — Yes, I'm buying it.
contrast_b_en: Do you have the keys? — I have them here.

title: Indirect object pronouns me, te, le, nos, os, les
micro_note: Indirect object pronouns mark 'to/for whom' an action happens. Even when the recipient is named with a + noun, Spanish almost always doubles it with le/les.
contrast_a: Le doy el libro a Ana.
contrast_a_en: I give the book to Ana.
contrast_b_en: They write to us every week.

title: Comparative of superiority/inferiority más/menos... que
micro_note: Form regular comparisons with más/menos + adjective/adverb/noun + que. Before a number in an affirmative sentence, use de instead of que (más de diez).
contrast_a: Madrid es más grande que Sevilla.
contrast_a_en: Madrid is bigger than Seville.
contrast_b_en: I waited more than twenty minutes.

title: Comparative of equality tan... como and tanto... como
micro_note: Use tan + adjective/adverb + como ('as ... as'). Use tanto/tanta/tantos/tantas + noun + como ('as much/many ... as'), agreeing with the noun.
contrast_a: Este café es tan bueno como aquel.
contrast_a_en: This coffee is as good as that one.
contrast_b_en: She has as many books as you.

title: Irregular comparatives mejor, peor, mayor, menor
micro_note: Bueno->mejor, malo->peor, grande->mayor (age/importance), pequeño->menor (age). Never say 'más bueno' for quality or 'más mejor'.
contrast_a: Esta ruta es mejor que la otra.
contrast_a_en: This route is better than the other.
contrast_b: Mi hermana mayor vive en Lima.
contrast_b_en: My older sister lives in Lima.

title: Double negatives with nada, nadie, ningún
micro_note: Spanish requires negative concord: when nada, nadie, or ningún follows the verb, keep no before the verb. Ninguno shortens to ningún before masculine singular nouns.
contrast_a: No veo a nadie en la plaza.
contrast_a_en: I don't see anyone in the square.
contrast_b_en: I don't have any problem.

title: Algo, alguien, algún vs nada, nadie, ningún
micro_note: Alguien/nadie refer to people (take personal a as direct objects); algo/nada to things; algún/ningún precede nouns and agree in gender.
contrast_a_en: Is anyone in the office?
contrast_b_en: I need to buy some gift.

title: Desde, hasta, de... a for time spans
micro_note: Use de... a with specific hours or days (de nueve a cinco), and desde... hasta when including articles or wider bounds (desde el lunes hasta el viernes).
contrast_a: La tienda abre de nueve a dos.
contrast_a_en: The shop opens from nine to two.
contrast_b: Trabajo desde las ocho hasta las cuatro.
contrast_b_en: I work from eight until four.

title: Doler, encantar, interesar, parecer
micro_note: Like gustar, doler (ache), encantar (love), interesar (interest), and parecer (seem) agree with the thing causing the feeling, with the person as indirect object.
contrast_a_en: My head hurts a lot.
contrast_b_en: We love these landscapes.

title: Polite requests with ¿Puedes...? and ¿Me das...?
micro_note: In everyday Spanish, polite requests use present indicative ¿Puedes + infinitive? or ¿Me das/pones...? (at cafés/shops) rather than harsh commands.
contrast_a_en: Could you get me a coffee with milk?
contrast_b_en: Can you close the window?

title: Para for destination, deadline, and recipient
micro_note: Para points forward toward a goal: recipient ('for Ana'), destination ('heading to Madrid'), deadline ('by Friday'), and purpose (+ infinitive, 'in order to').
contrast_a_en: The train leaves for Valencia.
contrast_b_en: I study in order to speak fluently.

title: Por for cause, price, duration, and route
micro_note: Por points to cause/reason ('because of'), exchange/price, duration ('for two hours'), movement through/along a place, and parts of the day (por la tarde).
contrast_a_en: We walked through the park.
contrast_b: Pagué diez euros por el libro.
contrast_b_en: I paid ten euros for the book.

title: Adverbs of manner in -mente
micro_note: Form manner adverbs by adding -mente to the feminine singular adjective (rápida -> rápidamente). Keep any original accent mark on the adjective.
contrast_a_en: Speak slowly, please.
contrast_b_en: She solved the case easily.

title: Neuter demonstratives esto, eso, aquello
micro_note: Esto, eso, and aquello never take a noun and have no gender or plural; they refer to an unnamed object, an entire idea, or a previous statement.
contrast_a_en: This seems very interesting to me.
contrast_b_en: Why do you say that?

title: Neuter article lo + adjective for abstract nouns
micro_note: Place lo before a masculine singular adjective to mean 'the [adjective] thing/part' (lo bueno, lo importante, lo difícil).
contrast_a_en: The important thing is to participate.
contrast_b: Lo mejor del viaje fue la comida.
contrast_b_en: The best part of the trip was the food.

title: Pretérito perfecto (he + participio) for recent past
micro_note: Form haber (he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, han) + past participle (-ado/-ido) for actions in an unfinished time frame (hoy, esta semana, alguna vez).
contrast_a_en: Today I have worked a lot.
contrast_b_en: Have you ever traveled to Peru?

title: Core irregular past participles (hecho, visto, dicho, escrito)
micro_note: Memorize the essential irregular participles: abrir->abierto, decir->dicho, escribir->escrito, hacer->hecho, morir->muerto, poner->puesto, romper->roto, ver->visto, volver->vuelto.
contrast_a_en: I have written a long letter.
contrast_b_en: Have you seen my keys today?

title: Ya / todavía no with present perfect
micro_note: Ya ('already') pairs with completed actions; todavía no / aún no ('not yet') indicates an expected action still pending.
contrast_a_en: I have already finished the report.
contrast_b_en: We have not had dinner yet.

title: Superlative el/la más... de
micro_note: Form the relative superlative with definite article + (noun) + más/menos + adjective + de (never 'en') for the group or place.
contrast_a: Es el río más largo del país.
contrast_a_en: It is the longest river in the country.
contrast_b: Es la calle menos ruidosa del barrio.
contrast_b_en: It is the least noisy street in the neighborhood.

title: Absolute superlative -ísimo / -ísima
micro_note: Add -ísimo/-ísima to an adjective stem to express 'extremely'. Spelling adapts where needed: rico->riquísimo, largo->larguísimo, feliz->felicísimo.
contrast_a_en: The soup is extraordinarily delicious.
contrast_b_en: The road is extremely long.

title: Impersonal se for general rules and signs
micro_note: Se + third-person singular/plural verb expresses 'one / people / you (general)' for instructions, customs, and signs without naming an agent.
contrast_a_en: Spanish is spoken here.
contrast_b_en: How do you say this in Spanish?

title: Basic relative pronoun que ('that / who / which')
micro_note: Que is the workhorse relative pronoun for both people and things, and unlike English it can NEVER be omitted in Spanish.
contrast_a: El libro que leo es genial.
contrast_a_en: The book (that) I'm reading is great.
contrast_b: La persona que llamó es mi tía.
contrast_b_en: The person who called is my aunt.

title: Exclamations with ¡Qué + adjective/noun!
micro_note: Use ¡Qué + adjective/adverb! ('How ...!') or ¡Qué + noun (+ más/tan + adjective)! ('What a ...!'). Omit un/una in these exclamations.
contrast_a_en: What a good idea you have!
contrast_b_en: How fast time passes!

title: Regular -ar preterite (pretérito indefinido)
micro_note: Use the preterite for completed, bounded past actions (ayer, el año pasado). Regular -ar endings: -é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -asteis, -aron. Watch the accent on -é and -ó!
contrast_a_en: I spoke with Pedro yesterday.
contrast_b_en: They bought a new house.

title: Regular -er / -ir preterite
micro_note: Regular -er and -ir verbs share identical preterite endings: -í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -isteis, -ieron.
contrast_a_en: I ate paella in Valencia.
contrast_b_en: They left very early today.

title: Spelling changes -car, -gar, -zar in yo preterite
micro_note: Before -é in the yo preterite, keep the original consonant sound: c->qu (busqué), g->gu (llegué), z->c (empecé). All other persons are regular.
contrast_a_en: I arrived home at midnight.
contrast_b_en: I started studying in March.

title: Ir and ser shared preterite (fui, fuiste, fue)
micro_note: Ir and ser have identical preterite forms: fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron. Context (destination with a vs description) instantly tells them apart.
contrast_a_en: I went to the concert on Friday.
contrast_b_en: The concert was unforgettable.

title: Strong u-stem preterites (tuv-, estuv-, pud-, pus-, sup-)
micro_note: High-frequency strong preterites switch to a u-stem and take unstressed endings (-e, -iste, -o, -imos, -isteis, -ieron) with NO accent marks.
contrast_a: Tuve un problema con el tren.
contrast_a_en: I had a problem with the train.
contrast_b_en: They could not open the box.

title: Strong i-stem and j-stem preterites (hic-, vin-, quis-, dij-, traj-)
micro_note: Hacer (hice/hizo), venir (vine), querer (quise) take i-stems; decir (dije), traer (traje), conducir (conduje) take j-stems with -eron (not -ieron) in ellos.
contrast_a_en: She told me the whole truth.
contrast_b_en: They brought flowers to dinner.

title: Third-person stem changes in -ir preterite (pidió, durmió)
micro_note: Stem-changing -ir verbs shift e->i or o->u ONLY in the third person (él/ellos) of the preterite: pidió/pidieron, durmió/durmieron, sintió/sintieron.
contrast_a_en: He slept ten hours straight.
contrast_b_en: They ordered two black coffees.

title: Third-person -y- preterite (leyó, oyó, construyó)
micro_note: When an -er/-ir stem ends in a vowel, intervocalic i turns to y in él/ellos preterite (leyó, leyeron, cayó, oyó), and other forms carry an accent on í.
contrast_a: Leyó toda la carta en silencio.
contrast_a_en: She read the whole letter in silence.
contrast_b: Oyeron un ruido en el techo.
contrast_b_en: They heard a noise on the roof.

title: Regular -ar imperfect (-aba) and -er/-ir imperfect (-ía)
micro_note: Use the imperfect for past habits ('used to'), ongoing backgrounds, ages, time, and descriptions. -ar takes -aba; -er/-ir take -ía.
contrast_a: De niño jugaba en la calle.
contrast_a_en: As a child I used to play in the street.
contrast_b_en: We lived in a small town.

title: The only three irregular imperfects: ser, ir, ver
micro_note: Spanish has ONLY three irregular imperfect verbs: ser (era), ir (iba), and ver (veía). Every other verb in the language is completely regular in the imperfect.
contrast_a: Íbamos a la playa cada verano.
contrast_a_en: We used to go to the beach every summer.
contrast_b_en: It was a very quiet night.

title: Interrupted action: imperfect background + preterite event
micro_note: Set the ongoing scene with imperfect (or estaba + gerundio) and cut into it with the interrupting completed event in the preterite.
contrast_a_en: It was raining hard when I went out.
contrast_b_en: I was cooking when the phone rang.

title: Completed chain of events vs static description
micro_note: Advance a story's plot step by step with preterite verbs; pause the action to describe appearance, weather, mood, or time with imperfect.
contrast_a: Entró, miró el reloj y se sentó.
contrast_a_en: He entered, checked his watch, and sat down.
contrast_b: La sala estaba vacía y hacía frío.
contrast_b_en: The room was empty and it was cold.

title: Meaning shift of saber, conocer, poder, querer in preterite
micro_note: In the preterite these verbs mark a turning point: supe (found out), conocí (met), pude (managed to), no quise (refused). In imperfect they express ongoing past states.
contrast_a_en: I met Laura in Seville.
contrast_b: Ya conocía a Laura desde antes.
contrast_b_en: I already knew Laura from before.

title: Pretérito perfecto vs indefinido time frames
micro_note: In Peninsular Spanish, use pretérito perfecto for unfinished periods (hoy, esta semana) and indefinido for finished ones (ayer, el año pasado).
contrast_a: Esta mañana he hablado con él.
contrast_a_en: This morning I have spoken with him.
contrast_b: Ayer hablé con él por teléfono.
contrast_b_en: Yesterday I spoke with him by phone.

title: Double object pronouns (indirect before direct)
micro_note: When both object pronouns appear together, indirect ALWAYS precedes direct (me lo, te la, nos los). Both stay together before the verb or attached to an infinitive/gerund.
contrast_a_en: She explained it to me calmly.
contrast_b_en: I am going to give it to you tomorrow.

title: Le/les -> se before lo/la/los/las
micro_note: Whenever third-person indirect le or les sits immediately before lo, la, los, or las, it transforms into se (se lo, se la) to avoid tongue-twisting l-sounds.
contrast_a: Se lo envié por correo ayer.
contrast_a_en: I sent it to him/her by email yesterday.
contrast_b: Se las presté a mis vecinos.
contrast_b_en: I lent them to my neighbors.

title: Pronoun attachment and accent marks on infinitives/gerunds
micro_note: Attaching one or two pronouns to a gerund or two pronouns to an infinitive requires adding a written accent to preserve original word stress (dándomelo, decírtelo).
contrast_a_en: I am explaining it to you now.
contrast_b_en: I want to buy it for myself soon.

title: Affirmative tú commands (regular)
micro_note: Regular affirmative tú commands simply use the third-person singular present indicative form (habla, come, escribe). Attach object pronouns to the end.
contrast_a_en: Listen to this new song.
contrast_b_en: Give it to me when you finish.

title: Eight irregular affirmative tú commands
micro_note: Eight short verbs have irregular affirmative tú commands: ven, di, sal, haz, ten, ve, pon, sé. Memorize them as a rhythm: ven di sal haz ten ve pon sé.
contrast_a: Haz la cama antes de salir.
contrast_a_en: Make the bed before leaving.
contrast_b: Ven aquí un segundo, por favor.
contrast_b_en: Come here a second, please.

title: Affirmative usted and ustedes commands
micro_note: Form usted/ustedes commands by swapping the present-tense vowel (-ar -> -e/-en, -er/-ir -> -a/-an) from the yo stem: hable, coma, venga, ponga.
contrast_a_en: Sign here, please. (usted)
contrast_b_en: Come in and sit down, everyone.

title: Negative tú commands (no + present subjunctive)
micro_note: Negative commands NEVER use the affirmative tú form. Use no + yo-stem with swapped vowel (-ar -> -es, -er/-ir -> -as), and place pronouns BEFORE the verb.
contrast_a_en: Speak louder.
contrast_b_en: Don't speak so quietly.

title: Acabar de + infinitive ('have just done')
micro_note: Present acabar de + infinitive means 'have just done'; imperfect acababa de + infinitive means 'had just done'.
contrast_a: Acabo de llegar a la estación.
contrast_a_en: I have just arrived at the station.
contrast_b_en: I had just closed when you called.

title: Volver a + infinitive ('to do again')
micro_note: Instead of repeating 'otra vez', Spanish often expresses repetition using conjugated volver + a + infinitive.
contrast_a: Voy a volver a leer el capítulo.
contrast_a_en: I am going to reread the chapter.
contrast_b: Nunca volvió a mencionar el tema.
contrast_b_en: He never brought up the topic again.

title: Empezar a / comenzar a / terminar de + infinitive
micro_note: Starting verbs take preposition a before an infinitive (empezar a, ponerse a); finishing or stopping verbs take de (terminar de, dejar de).
contrast_a_en: It started to rain at noon.
contrast_b: Dejé de fumar hace dos años.
contrast_b_en: I quit smoking two years ago.

title: Seguir / continuar + gerundio ('keep doing')
micro_note: Use seguir or continuar directly + gerundio to express continuing an action, or seguir sin + infinitive for 'still haven't done'.
contrast_a_en: It is still raining since last night.
contrast_b_en: I still haven't found my glasses.

title: Llevar + time + gerundio ('have been doing for X time')
micro_note: Llevar + duration + gerundio expresses how long an ongoing action has lasted. Replace gerundio with sin + infinitive for how long you haven't done something.
contrast_a_en: I have been studying Spanish for three months.
contrast_b: Lleva dos días sin dormir bien.
contrast_b_en: He has gone two days without sleeping well.

title: Hace + duration + que + present ('have been for X')
micro_note: Hace + time + que + present tense (or present + desde hace + time) expresses actions that began in the past and continue right into the present.
contrast_a: Hace dos años que vivo aquí.
contrast_a_en: I have been living here for two years.
contrast_b: Vivo aquí desde hace dos años.
contrast_b_en: I have been living here for two years.

title: Preterite + hace + duration ('X time ago')
micro_note: When paired with a preterite verb, hace + time expression means 'ago'—marking a completed moment in the past.
contrast_a: Llegamos a Madrid hace una semana.
contrast_a_en: We arrived in Madrid a week ago.
contrast_b: Vi esa película hace mucho tiempo.
contrast_b_en: I saw that movie a long time ago.

title: Simple future (regular verbs)
micro_note: Attach -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án directly onto the FULL infinitive of -ar, -er, and -ir verbs. Used for predictions, promises, and formal plans.
contrast_a_en: Tomorrow I will speak with the director.
contrast_b_en: They will live near the coast.

title: Irregular future stems (tendr-, podr-, har-, dir-, sabr-)
micro_note: Twelve verbs shorten or insert -d- in the future stem before the regular endings: tendré, vendré, pondré, saldré, valdré, podré, sabré, querré, cabré, habré, haré, diré.
contrast_a_en: We will have more time on Monday.
contrast_b_en: I will tell you the answer soon.

title: Future of probability in the present ('must be / probably')
micro_note: Spanish frequently uses the simple future to guess or speculate about the PRESENT ('I wonder where he is / He must be at home').
contrast_a_en: Where could Juan be right now?
contrast_b_en: He is probably still at work.

title: First conditional: Si + present, present / future / imperative
micro_note: Real/likely conditions use si + present indicative in the if-clause (NEVER future after si!) and present, future, or imperative in the result clause.
contrast_a: Si llueve, nos quedamos en casa.
contrast_a_en: If it rains, we stay home.
contrast_b_en: If you finish early, call me.

title: Simple conditional (-ía) for polite requests and advice
micro_note: Add -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían to the full infinitive (same 12 irregular stems as future). Ideal for polite wishes (me gustaría) and advice (yo que tú...).
contrast_a_en: I would like to book a table.
contrast_b_en: You should rest a little more.

title: Adjectives that change meaning with ser vs estar
micro_note: Key adjectives shift meaning sharply: ser listo (clever) vs estar listo (ready); ser aburrido (boring) vs estar aburrido (bored); ser rico (wealthy) vs estar rico (tasty).
contrast_a_en: This movie is very boring.
contrast_b_en: I am very bored at home.

title: Estar + past participle for resulting states
micro_note: Pair estar with a past participle agreeing in gender and number to describe the state resulting from a prior action (cerrado, roto, hecho, cansado).
contrast_a_en: The window is broken.
contrast_b_en: The letters are already written.

title: Stressed possessive pronouns mío, tuyo, suyo, nuestro
micro_note: Stressed possessives follow the noun ('un amigo mío') or stand alone with an article ('el mío') to replace a previously mentioned noun.
contrast_a: Es una amiga mía del trabajo.
contrast_a_en: She is a friend of mine from work.
contrast_b: Tu coche es rojo; el mío es azul.
contrast_b_en: Your car is red; mine is blue.

title: Por vs para contrastive precision
micro_note: Use para for destination, purpose, deadline, and recipient; use por for cause, exchange, duration, means, and path. Switching them changes meaning completely.
contrast_a_en: I work for a local company.
contrast_b_en: I am covering for my sick colleague.

title: Reciprocal se/nos ('each other')
micro_note: Plural reflexive pronouns nos, os, se express mutual actions between two or more people ('each other'). Add mutuamente or el uno al otro for clarity.
contrast_a_en: We write to each other every day.
contrast_b: Se abrazaron al llegar al aeropuerto.
contrast_b_en: They hugged each other at the airport.

title: Meaning-changing pronominal verbs (ir/irse, dormir/dormirse)
micro_note: Adding se often marks initiation or departure: ir (go to) vs irse (leave), dormir (sleep) vs dormirse (fall asleep), quedar (meet/remain) vs quedarse (stay).
contrast_a_en: I am going to the cinema with Marta.
contrast_b: Me voy ya porque es tarde.
contrast_b_en: I am leaving now because it's late.

title: Aspectual se of total consumption (comerse, beberse, leerse)
micro_note: Adding a reflexive pronoun to verbs of eating, drinking, or reading emphasizes completing the entire quantified object ('ate the whole thing').
contrast_a_en: I ate pizza yesterday.
contrast_b: Se comió toda la pizza solo.
contrast_b_en: He ate the entire pizza by himself.

title: Pluscuamperfecto (había + participio) for past before past
micro_note: Use imperfect haber (había, habías, había...) + past participle to place an event earlier than another past reference point ('had already done').
contrast_a: Cuando llegué, el tren ya había salido.
contrast_a_en: When I arrived, the train had already left.
contrast_b_en: I had never seen so much snow.

title: Ponerse + adjective for sudden emotional/physical shifts
micro_note: Ponerse + adjective expresses a rapid, involuntary change in mood, health, or appearance (ponerse nervioso, rojo, contento, enfermo).
contrast_a: Se puso muy contento al oírlo.
contrast_a_en: He got very happy upon hearing it.
contrast_b: Me pongo nervioso antes de volar.
contrast_b_en: I get nervous before flying.

title: Hacerse + noun/adjective for deliberate or natural change
micro_note: Hacerse expresses voluntary changes (profession, religion, ideology) or natural progressions like hacerse de noche or hacerse rico.
contrast_a: Se hizo arquitecta tras cinco años.
contrast_a_en: She became an architect after five years.
contrast_b: En invierno se hace de noche pronto.
contrast_b_en: In winter it gets dark early.

title: Volverse + adjective for lasting personality/state changes
micro_note: Volverse signals a deeper, often involuntary or negative transformation in character or state (volverse loco, desconfiado, insoportable).
contrast_a: Con el tiempo se volvió muy paciente.
contrast_a_en: Over time he became very patient.
contrast_b: Casi me vuelvo loco buscando las llaves.
contrast_b_en: I nearly went crazy looking for the keys.

title: Quedarse + adjective/participle for resulting permanent/reaction states
micro_note: Quedarse describes a state left behind after an event or shock (quedarse sorprendido, callado, solo, ciego, sin dinero).
contrast_a: Se quedó sorprendido con el premio.
contrast_a_en: He was left astonished by the prize.
contrast_b: Nos quedamos sin batería en el viaje.
contrast_b_en: We ended up out of battery on the trip.

title: Accidental se (se + indirect pronoun + verb)
micro_note: Spanish softens blame for accidents using se + me/te/le/nos + third-person verb agreeing with the object: 'se me cayó el vaso' ('the glass slipped from me').
contrast_a_en: I broke the plate.
contrast_b: Se me rompió el plato sin querer.
contrast_b_en: The plate accidentally broke on me.

title: Pasiva refleja (se + 3rd person verb agreeing with noun)
micro_note: When no agent is mentioned, Spanish strongly prefers pasiva refleja over ser + participle: match the verb to singular or plural subject (se vende casa / se venden casas).
contrast_a_en: A central apartment is for rent.
contrast_b: Se venden entradas en la taquilla.
contrast_b_en: Tickets are sold at the box office.

title: Indirect speech in present reporting frame (dice que...)
micro_note: When the reporting verb is present or present perfect (dice que, ha dicho que), keep the original verb tense and update only pronouns and place/time pointers.
contrast_a_en: Ana says: 'I am going tomorrow.'
contrast_b_en: Ana says that she is going tomorrow.

title: Indirect yes/no questions with preguntar si
micro_note: Report a yes/no question using preguntar si (without accent on si!) instead of que.
contrast_a_en: He asked me: 'Do you have time?'
contrast_b_en: He asked me if I had time.

title: Indirect wh-questions retaining written accents
micro_note: Indirect questions keep the written accent on qué, dónde, cuándo, cómo, quién, even without question marks.
contrast_a: No sé dónde dejé mi abrigo.
contrast_a_en: I don't know where I left my coat.
contrast_b_en: Ask her when the flight arrives.

title: Contrast with pero vs sino / sino que
micro_note: Use pero to add a limitation. Use sino after a negative statement to replace and correct it ('not X, but rather Y'); use sino que before a conjugated verb.
contrast_a_en: He is not a doctor, but rather a nurse.
contrast_b: No solo lee, sino que también escribe.
contrast_b_en: She not only reads, but also writes.

title: Consecutive connectors así que, por eso, entonces
micro_note: Link a cause to its natural consequence using por eso ('that's why'), así que ('so'), or entonces ('then'). All take the indicative.
contrast_a: Estaba cansado, así que me acosté.
contrast_a_en: I was tired, so I went to bed.
contrast_b: Llovió mucho; por eso no salimos.
contrast_b_en: It rained a lot; that's why we didn't go out.

title: Temporal clauses with cuando + indicative (habits & past)
micro_note: Use cuando + indicative for habitual routines (cuando llueve...) and completed past events (cuando llegué...). Future reference switches to subjunctive!
contrast_a: Cuando llego a casa, preparo té.
contrast_a_en: Whenever I get home, I make tea.
contrast_b_en: When I arrived, they were already dining.

title: Mientras for simultaneous actions
micro_note: Mientras ('while') links two parallel actions. Use imperfect for simultaneous past backgrounds, or present for current/habitual overlap.
contrast_a_en: I listen to the radio while I cook.
contrast_b_en: While I was reading, he was painting.

title: Al + infinitive ('upon / when doing')
micro_note: Al + infinitive cleanly compresses 'when [subject] did/does something' into a crisp two-word time clause.
contrast_a: Al abrir la puerta vi una carta.
contrast_a_en: Upon opening the door I saw a letter.
contrast_b_en: When we arrived at the town we rested.

title: Antes de / después de + infinitive (same subject)
micro_note: When both clauses share the same subject, use antes de + infinitive or después de + infinitive instead of a finite clause with que.
contrast_a: Lávate las manos antes de comer.
contrast_a_en: Wash your hands before eating.
contrast_b: Después de cenar salimos a caminar.
contrast_b_en: After having dinner we went for a walk.

title: Para + infinitive (same-subject purpose)
micro_note: Express purpose with para + infinitive whenever the subject of the main verb and the purpose action are identical.
contrast_a: Ahorro dinero para viajar en julio.
contrast_a_en: I save money to travel in July.
contrast_b_en: I came early to talk with you.

title: Sin + infinitive ('without doing')
micro_note: Spanish uses sin + infinitive (NEVER gerundio!) where English uses 'without + -ing'.
contrast_a_en: He left without closing the window.
contrast_b_en: She speaks Spanish without overthinking.

title: Por + infinitive ('for / because of doing')
micro_note: Por + infinitive gives the reason behind gratitude, apologies, or consequences ('thanks for coming', 'for arriving late').
contrast_a_en: Thanks for coming so soon.
contrast_b_en: Sorry for interrupting your call.

title: Relative donde and cuando with antecedents
micro_note: Use donde ('where') after a place noun and cuando ('when') after a time noun without accent marks.
contrast_a: Es el café donde nos conocimos.
contrast_a_en: It's the café where we met.
contrast_b: Recuerdo el día cuando nevó aquí.
contrast_b_en: I remember the day when it snowed here.

title: Preposition + quien / quienes for human antecedents
micro_note: After prepositions like con, para, de, or a referring to people, use quien (singular) or quienes (plural).
contrast_a: La amiga con quien vivo es médica.
contrast_a_en: The friend with whom I live is a doctor.
contrast_b_en: They are people whom I trust.

title: Lo que ('what / that which') as headless relative
micro_note: Lo que replaces 'what' inside a statement (not a question!) to mean 'the thing that' or 'everything that'.
contrast_a_en: I don't understand what you are saying.
contrast_b: Haz lo que te parezca mejor.
contrast_b_en: Do what seems best to you.

title: Present subjunctive formation (regular vowel swap)
micro_note: Form present subjunctive from the yo present stem and swap the thematic vowel: -ar takes -e/-es/-e/-emos/-éis/-en; -er/-ir take -a/-as/-a/-amos/-áis/-an.
contrast_a: Hablas claro. -> Quiero que hables claro.
contrast_a_en: You speak clearly. -> I want you to speak clearly.
contrast_b: Vives aquí. -> Espero que vivas bien.
contrast_b_en: You live here. -> I hope you live well.

title: Core irregular present subjunctives (DISHES)
micro_note: Six essential irregular present subjunctives: dar (dé), ir (vaya), ser (sea), haber (haya), estar (esté), saber (sepa).
contrast_a_en: I hope you are feeling better tomorrow.
contrast_b_en: Hopefully there will be sun this Sunday.

title: Wishes with Ojalá (que) + present subjunctive
micro_note: Ojalá + present subjunctive expresses warm hopes and realistic wishes ('hopefully / I hope that'). Que is optional.
contrast_a_en: Hopefully we arrive on time.
contrast_b_en: I hope you like the gift.

title: Desire/influence with querer / esperar que + subjunctive
micro_note: When the subject of querer, esperar, or preferir wants SOMEONE ELSE to act, use que + subjunctive. Same subject stays with an infinitive!
contrast_a_en: I want to study tonight.
contrast_b_en: I want you to study tonight.

title: Impersonal necessity with es necesario / importante que + subjunctive
micro_note: General impersonal statements take an infinitive ('es importante dormir'). Adding a specific subject with que triggers the subjunctive.
contrast_a_en: It is important to drink water.
contrast_b_en: It is important that you drink water.

title: Future time clauses with cuando + present subjunctive
micro_note: Whenever cuando points to an action that HAS NOT HAPPENED YET (future time), Spanish obligates the present subjunctive—never future tense!
contrast_a_en: When you arrive, let me know please.
contrast_b: Te llamaré cuando termine la clase.
contrast_b_en: I will call you when class ends.

title: Possibility with puede que + present subjunctive
micro_note: Puede que ('it may be that / maybe') ALWAYS triggers the subjunctive, whereas a lo mejor always takes the indicative.
contrast_a_en: It might rain this afternoon.
contrast_b: A lo mejor llueve esta tarde.
contrast_b_en: Maybe it will rain this afternoon.

title: Soler + infinitive for habitual actions
micro_note: Soler (suelo, sueles... in present; solía in imperfect) translates 'usually do / used to usually do'. It is never used in preterite or future.
contrast_a_en: I usually have breakfast at seven.
contrast_b_en: Before, we used to go to the theater.

title: Deber de + infinitive for supposition vs deber for duty
micro_note: Deber + infinitive expresses moral obligation ('must/should'); deber de + infinitive expresses logical probability ('must be').
contrast_a_en: You must hand in the text today.
contrast_b: Debe de ser muy tarde ya.
contrast_b_en: It must be very late already.

title: Article omission with uncountable nouns and plural generics
micro_note: Drop articles after verbs like tener, buscar, comprar, and haber when referring to unspecified quantities, professions, or uncountable substances.
contrast_a: Compro pan y leche cada día.
contrast_a_en: I buy bread and milk every day.
contrast_b: El pan de esta panadería es excelente.
contrast_b_en: The bread from this bakery is excellent.

title: Diminutives -ito / -cito for size and affection
micro_note: Diminutives soften tone, express affection, or shrink size (cafecito, ratito, cerquita). Words ending in -n/-r/-e often take -cito.
contrast_a_en: Wait just a little moment, please.
contrast_b_en: Let's have a quick little coffee.

title: Pre-noun vs post-noun adjective nuance (viejo, pobre, nuevo)
micro_note: Certain adjectives shift meaning before a noun: un viejo amigo (longtime friend) vs un amigo viejo (elderly friend); un pobre hombre (unfortunate) vs un hombre pobre (penniless).
contrast_a: Es un viejo amigo de la escuela.
contrast_a_en: He is an old (longtime) friend from school.
contrast_b_en: She bought a brand-new car yesterday.

title: Indefinite pronouns cualquiera, cada, ambos, demás
micro_note: Cualquiera drops -a before a singular noun (cualquier día). Los/las demás means 'the rest/others'; ambos/ambas means 'both'.
contrast_a_en: You can call me any day.
contrast_b: Llegaron Ana y los demás invitados.
contrast_b_en: Ana and the rest of the guests arrived.
